assessment_summary: The statement claims that all T1 spaces are Hausdorff. This is false. A standard counterexample is an infinite set equipped with the cofinite topology. It is T1 because singletons have finite complements (size 1) so their complements are open, making singletons closed. It is not Hausdorff because the intersection of any two non-empty open sets has a finite complement, so it cannot be empty in an infinite space, making disjoint open neighborhoods impossible.
counterexample: Let X be an infinite set (e.g., the set of integers Z) equipped with the cofinite topology, where the open sets are the empty set and all subsets of X whose complement is finite. In this space, every singleton {x} is closed because its complement, X \ {x}, is open (since its complement is just {x}, which is a finite set). Thus, the space is T1. However, X is not Hausdorff. If U and V are open neighborhoods of two distinct points x and y, then both X \ U and X \ V are finite. By De Morgan's laws, X \ (U ∩ V) = (X \ U) ∪ (X \ V), which is the union of two finite sets and therefore finite. Since X is infinite, the complement of a finite set cannot be X, which means U ∩ V cannot be empty. Hence, x and y cannot have disjoint open neighborhoods.
